requirements.quote: All externally reachable API endpoints must authenticate each request with an OAuth2 or OpenID Connect bearer token issued by the corporate identity provider, or with mutual TLS.
Internal service calls must carry a mutual TLS client certificate or a signed workload identity token, and services must reject calls that carry neither.
Access tokens must expire within 15 minutes, and refresh tokens must be rotated every time they are used.
Any administrative or back-office access requires multi-factor authentication.
Passwords must be stored as salted hashes using argon2id or bcrypt only.
Login and token endpoints must throttle repeated failed attempts and apply a temporary lockout after ten consecutive failures.
For every request touching a customer-owned resource, the service must verify that the authenticated caller owns the resource or is explicitly entitled to it.
Internal users should be assigned roles appropriate to their job, and services should define role sets as needed.
Every service should connect to its database with a dedicated account that has only the grants it needs, and applications should avoid shared administrative credentials.
Administrative and debug endpoints must not be served on public networks and must be reachable only through the private administrative network.
Personal data held in databases and object storage must be encrypted at rest with AES-256 or stronger, using keys managed in the corporate key management service.
Primary account numbers must not be stored in clear text anywhere and must be replaced by tokens issued by the card token vault.
All external network traffic must use TLS 1.2 or higher, and plain HTTP listeners are not permitted.
Connections between services, and between services and data stores or brokers, must be encrypted in transit.
Only approved algorithms may be used, and MD5, SHA-1, DES, 3DES and ECB mode are prohibited.
Encryption keys must be stored in the key management service and never alongside the data they protect, and every key must be rotated at least once a year.
Services must verify TLS certificates on every connection and must not disable certificate verification.
Legacy partner integrations may continue to use TLS 1.0 until a migration date is agreed with Security Architecture.
Each service should limit the personal data it stores to what is reasonably required and document the purpose of its fields.
Each category of personal data should have a retention period, and an automated job should delete the data when the period ends.
Personal data may leave Meridian Pay only to a processor covered by an approved data processing agreement, and only the fields necessary for the purpose may be sent.
Non-production environments must not contain real personal data or card data, and synthetic or masked data must be used instead.
Reports and exports containing personal data should be made available only to authorized users and for a limited time.
Logs should not contain secrets, card numbers or personal data other than opaque identifiers.
Backups must be protected appropriately, and restoration from backup must be tested regularly.
Secrets must not be stored in source code, configuration files, API specifications or infrastructure definitions.
Services must obtain runtime secrets from the approved secret store when they start, and secrets must not be passed as plain environment variables in deployment manifests.
Every external input must be validated against a schema, and invalid requests must be rejected before processing.
External APIs should enforce a rate limit for each client and return HTTP 429 when the limit is exceeded.
Webhook payloads, inbound and outbound, must carry an HMAC signature that the receiver verifies together with a timestamp.
Error responses must not contain stack traces, SQL text or internal host names.
Database queries must be parameterized.
Service credentials must be rotated periodically and after suspected exposure.
Databases and message brokers must run in private subnets and must not have public endpoints.
Object storage buckets must have public access blocked.
SSH, RDP and database ports must not be open to 0.0.0.0/0.
Externally exposed APIs must be fronted by a web application firewall with rate limiting enabled.
Services that call third parties must restrict outbound traffic to an approved allowlist of destinations.
Authentication failures, privilege changes and access to sensitive data must be logged.
Audit logs must be stored in tamper-resistant storage and retained for an appropriate period.
Access to centralized logs should be restricted to personnel who need it.
Continuous integration must scan dependencies and container images, and critical findings must be fixed within 14 days.
Containers must run as a non-root user.
